Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier?
Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

Wenbo Huang1   Jianxin Bi1,2   Shunyu Yang1   Ruiyang Si1
Rui Ni1   Qiang Wang1   Shulong Jiang1   Yintianrun Zhang1
Feixiang Ruan1   Kewei Zhang1   Ye Huang1   Shukai Gong1   Daquan Zhou1,∗ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark’s success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark’s criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

Keywords: embodied agent, self-improvement, robot policy evaluation

1 Introduction

Agents that write code to control robots with multimodal language models complete many manipulation tasks zero-shot [19, 15, 12, 29], but preserve nothing from one episode to the next, which makes self-improvement across episodes a natural next step [28, 31, 36]. Such agents are developed and compared on embodied simulation benchmarks [9, 20, 22] originally built to evaluate end-to-end policies trained by imitating demonstrations, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models [6, 17, 4, 25] and world action models (WAMs) [26]. The actual success criteria of these benchmarks often ask for more than the instruction; in the press_by_number task of RoboDojo, for instance, the criteria require the blue button to be pressed exactly twice, between two groups of red presses, which the instruction never states (figure 1a). For policies trained by imitation, this gap is harmless, since their demonstrations already contain every detail the criteria verify: order, counts, end states, and the return of both arms. An agent that receives only the instruction, however, lacks this information. Existing self-improving methods therefore expose the criteria to the agent to different degrees, from rule descriptions [10] and published scoring tables [18, 13] to numeric thresholds [14], formal goal predicates [32], and the source code of the verifier [3]. A robot in the real world, by contrast, receives only its instruction and, at most, a success judged by a human or a VLM. Our research question is: when a self-improving embodied agent is exposed to the success criteria, does the code it iteratively produces better perform the instructed task, or simply overfit to the verification criteria?

Studies of benchmark validity and of specification gaming show that criteria can demand more than the instruction states and that agents exploit a verifier they can inspect [16, 40, 37], but we are not aware of work that measures how much of a reported gain in embodied self-improvement comes from reading the criteria, or whether it survives when the criteria change. We therefore compare two settings of one fixed self-improvement loop, in which a frozen coding agent acts and a learner agent turns its episodes into a library of skills and memory: with Criteria Exposure (w/ CE), the learner reads the criteria; without it (w/o CE), the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded. We ask three questions: on which tasks exposure raises the score; whether its lead survives a change of criteria, both of the criteria that judge the episodes and of the criteria the learner reads; and whether what it adds carries over to new tasks and to two further benchmarks, LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365. To change the criteria, we rewrite them for the RoboDojo tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction, so that they verify only what the instruction asks. On these tasks every episode is judged by both versions, and in a separate run the learner reads the rewritten criteria instead of the original ones.

Our experiments reveal three findings. First, under the original criteria, exposure helps only on tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction; when criteria and instruction agree, learning from success alone does just as well. Second, the score of exposure follows the criteria it read: when the same episodes are judged by instruction-faithful criteria, its advantage disappears, as the exposed libraries lose successes while the success-only libraries gain them (figure 1b); conversely, a library learned from the rewritten criteria scores far lower when judged by the original ones. Third, the lead of exposure does not reappear on new RoboDojo tasks, and across benchmarks neither the exposed nor the success-only library gives a clear gain over the empty library; only experience gathered within the target benchmark does.

Taken together, these results suggest a practical principle for evaluating embodied self-improvement: the learner should receive only the feedback a robot would receive in the real world, and the benchmark’s criteria should verify what the instruction says. A gain that holds when the criteria are changed but still agree with the instruction reflects what the agent has learned about the task. Seen this way, whether the learner reads the criteria is not an implementation detail of a self-improving agent but a choice about measurement, and it determines what a reported gain means.

2 Related Work

Code-writing embodied agents and their benchmarks. Language models plan and act for robots by selecting skills [1], writing policy code [19], or composing value maps [15]; recent agents close the loop with code replanning and thin tool layers [12, 29, 13], and frontier models now control robots zero-shot. These agents are evaluated on benchmarks built for vision-language-action policies trained on demonstrations [6, 17, 4, 25]: RoboDojo [9], LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO [20, 38], RoboCasa365 [22], and RoboTwin 2.0 [8]. These works score agents with criteria written for demonstration-trained policies; whether the criteria verify only what the instruction asks is rarely examined on its own, and we measure how this gap enters the score of a self-improving agent.

Self-improving agents and the feedback their learners see. In digital domains, programs are evolved against automatic evaluators [23, 34], agents reflect on textual feedback [28, 36], skills are verified in a game world [31], and code is revised against tests [33]. Embodied systems differ in how much of the success criteria their learners or agents see. Some give only success or keep the grader isolated [27, 21]; others add rule descriptions with coarse feedback [10], published scoring tables and partial numeric thresholds [18, 13, 14], formal goal predicates [32], or the source code of the verifier [3]. In RATs, the verifier reads goal predicates and ground truth while the policy writer’s side is filtered [35]. In these systems the amount of criteria information is mostly fixed by design rather than varied as an experimental factor. The closest comparison is an ablation of EmbodiedEvo between task descriptions alone and descriptions with the wiki, but both arms are judged by the original criteria [18]. We treat exposure as the variable and test what it gains under a second set of criteria.

Specification gaming and benchmark validity. Optimizing a proxy diverges from the intended objective [2, 30], with measurable effects of reward misspecification [24]. Language agents exploit tests and evaluators they can inspect [37, 5], and agentic benchmarks need checks of their own validity [16, 40]. Where rule-based criteria are missing, success is judged by VLMs [11] or by autonomous real-world evaluation [39]. Building on these studies, we further show that on embodied benchmarks the act of reading the criteria turns the gap between criteria and instruction into score, and we measure this share with counterfactual criteria that score the same instructions.

3 Preliminaries and Study Design

This section describes the controlled study we use to analyze what a self-improving embodied agent learns from the success criteria. The study compares two settings of one loop, w/ CE and w/o CE, and answers three questions: where exposure raises the score under the original criteria, whether the advantage holds when the criteria change, and whether the library carries over to new tasks and benchmarks. We describe in turn the loop and its two settings, criteria-limited tasks, instruction-faithful criteria, and the evaluation protocol.

3.1 Self-Improvement Loop and Criteria Exposure

A task τ=(Iτ,Dτ,Cτ)\tau=(I_{\tau},D_{\tau},C_{\tau}) has an instruction IτI_{\tau}, a distribution of layouts DτD_{\tau} and success criteria CτC_{\tau} that judge each trajectory; some benchmarks also report a score and stages. The success the instruction asks for, SτS_{\tau}, is defined by IτI_{\tau} and cannot be computed directly. A frozen actor π\pi, GPT-6 Astra with high reasoning effort, acts through the primitives of PyRUA-Lean [29]. In each round a learner UU, Claude Code with Opus 5.5 and high reasoning effort, makes one revision of the library ℒ\mathcal{L}, a set of callable skills and memory entries, from the evidence Ev​(B)E_{v}(B) of the last batch, and the revision is rolled back if the batch clearly regresses. Each task has its own library, learned over five rounds on five development layouts. Algorithm 1 and figure 2 summarize the loop for one task.

The loop runs in two settings. Without Criteria Exposure (w/o CE), the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded; the criteria code, the score and the stages are withheld. A robot in the real world has no criteria code and receives success from a human or a VLM, so this is the setting in simulation closest to the real world. With Criteria Exposure (w/ CE), the learner also reads the criteria code of the task and the score and stages of each episode, as systems that give the learner the source of the verifier do; the actor never reads them. The actor, the primitives, perception and benchmark scoring are frozen and only the library changes; the two settings share the loop and differ in what the learner reads, so differences between them reflect exposure rather than the loop itself.

3.2 Criteria-limited Tasks

We call a task criteria-limited if CτC_{\tau} disagrees with SτS_{\tau} on some trajectories, either by rejecting a trajectory SτS_{\tau} accepts or by accepting one SτS_{\tau} rejects (criteria looser than the instruction); all other tasks are faithful. Such tasks appear in every benchmark we examined, RoboDojo, LIBERO [20] (whose instructions and goals LIBERO-PRO keeps), RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0 [8], and their disagreements fall into a few kinds. The criteria may ask for more than the instruction states, such as an order, a count or an end state: in RoboDojo, press_by_number requires a button protocol its instruction never gives. They may be stricter than the instruction needs, such as an unstated tolerance for an object resting on another in LIBERO. They may contradict the instruction, as in a LIBERO task that asks to stack a bowl on the front bowl while its criteria require the back one. Or they may verify less than the instruction asks: in RoboTwin 2.0, shake_bottle_horizontally succeeds once the bottle is lifted.

We rewrite criteria and re-judge episodes on RoboDojo only. Its criteria report a score and stages besides success, so an exposed learner reads the most complete information there, and we compared the criteria of all of its tasks with their instructions; rewriting the criteria of other benchmarks and repeating these experiments on them is left to future work. We distinguish seven types: hidden rules, hard thresholds, timing and irreversible events, criteria defects, extra end states, loose criteria, and contradictions. In RoboDojo, after a manual review of every task, the 20 criteria-limited tasks have 26 variants, and hidden rules and hard thresholds are the most common types. Criteria-limited is defined with respect to the instruction the agent receives at reset; the RoboDojo website publishes part of these rules in its task descriptions and scoring tables.

3.3 Instruction-faithful Criteria

For each criteria-limited task we rewrite only the criteria code, never the instruction, and leave the original repository untouched: hidden rules are removed or relaxed, defects fixed, hard thresholds relaxed to what still clearly satisfies the instruction, loose criteria tightened where the simulator state can detect the difference, and the return of both arms kept. The two criteria judged the same episodes independently, and every episode whose verdict flipped was checked by hand without finding a misjudgment by the new criteria. Each evaluation episode is then judged by both criteria, giving SRorig\text{SR}^{\text{orig}} and SRfaith\text{SR}^{\text{faith}}. Since both criteria score the same instruction on the same episode, any difference between the two success rates comes from what the criteria verify, not from behavior. CfaithC^{\text{faith}} is ours and serves as a proxy for SτS_{\tau}; we discuss this in section 5.

3.4 Experiment Settings and Evaluation Protocol

To isolate the effect of exposure, the two settings of each comparison use the same actor, primitives, round budget and development layouts. The 25 learned tasks comprise 16 criteria-limited and 9 faithful tasks, grouped in advance by whether their criteria were rewritten; Appendix A.4 lists the tasks. Development uses layouts 0–4 of seed 1 and testing layouts 0–19 of seed 0. We report the success rate (SR) and compare settings layout by layout. All experiments use the same actor and learner. To reuse libraries, we distill the libraries of ten source tasks into one shared library and apply it to disjoint target tasks, in RoboDojo and on two further benchmarks with aligned primitives.

We use three simulated benchmarks with different roles. RoboDojo is the main benchmark: its rule-based criteria report a score and stages, and all three questions are answered on it. LIBERO-PRO is a single-arm tabletop benchmark where zero-shot success is already near the ceiling; it tests whether transfer still has room at high scores. RoboCasa365 has household kitchen scenes and the lowest zero-shot scores; it tests cross-benchmark experience and also hosts in-benchmark learning.

4 Experiments and Analysis

We test three hypotheses:

  • •

    H1. Exposure raises the score only on tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction (section 4.1).

  • •

    H2. If exposure teaches the verifier rather than the task, its lead shrinks or reverses when the same episodes are judged by instruction-faithful criteria (section 4.2.1), and each exposed library scores best under whichever criteria its learner read (section 4.2.2).

  • •

    H3. What exposure adds does not carry over to new tasks or benchmarks (section 4.3).

4.1 Exposure under the Original Criteria

We first judge the benchmark’s way, by the original criteria, which are also the criteria the exposed learner reads.

4.1.1 Success-only versus Exposed Self-Improvement

Setup.

We learn one library per task and setting on the 25 learned tasks (16 criteria-limited, 9 faithful), over five rounds on five development layouts, and test each library on layouts 0–19 of seed 0 against the empty library. The two groups were fixed before any result was seen.

Results.

Table 1 and figure 3 show three patterns. First, learning from success alone doubles success, from 24.6% to 47.8%, and reading the criteria adds another 14.2 points (62.0%). Second, this extra gain comes from the criteria-limited tasks: on faithful tasks the two settings are level (83.3% and 80.6%), while on criteria-limited tasks exposure leads, 51.6% against 27.8%. Third, among criteria-limited tasks the lead depends on whether an unstated rule shows in failed episodes: in build_tower the leftover blocks reveal it and both settings reach 20/20, whereas the button protocol of press_by_number, blue pressed twice and between the two red groups, never shows, and the success-only learner never finds it.

4.1.2 Synthesis

  • •

    Exposure pays off only where the criteria ask for more than the instruction. Richer feedback is often assumed to make self-improvement better. Our results show a condition: when the criteria verify what the instruction says, success alone tells the learner what the task requires, and what remains, a reliable procedure, is learned equally well in both settings. Exposure helps only with rules that the instruction omits and that failures do not reveal.

  • •

    The advantage of exposure measures the benchmark as much as the agent. Because it comes from what the instruction leaves out, the gain of exposure grows with the gap between a benchmark’s instructions and its criteria. Some of what the criteria reveal is legitimate task knowledge, but it belongs in the instruction: benchmarks that state in the instruction what their criteria verify (counts, order, end states, the reset of the arms) and release versioned criteria with a comparison against the instructions would let self-improvement be compared on the task alone.

4.2 Changing the Criteria: Task or Verifier?

Section 4.1 judged with the criteria the exposed learner read. Changing them separates two explanations. If exposure teaches the task, its lead should survive under CfaithC^{\text{faith}}; if it teaches the verifier, the lead should shrink or reverse, and each library should score best under whichever criteria its learner read. We change the criteria used for judging and the criteria that are read.

4.2.1 Re-judging with Instruction-faithful Criteria

Setup.

We run the libraries of section 4.1.1 on the 16 learned criteria-limited tasks, all of which have rewritten criteria, 20 layouts each, and judge every episode by both criteria.

Results.

Figure 5 shows the lead of exposure disappear. Under CorigC^{\text{orig}} the exposed library leads, 51.6% against 27.8%: paired by task and layout, it alone succeeds on 93 layouts and the success-only library alone on 17. Judged by CfaithC^{\text{faith}}, the same episodes give 45.0% for the exposed library and 47.2% for the success-only one, a difference within noise (47 against 54 layouts); the gap shrinks by 25.9 points (95% bootstrap interval over tasks 4.7–54.4). The success-only library loses almost nothing: CfaithC^{\text{faith}} accepts all but 2 of its 89 successes under CorigC^{\text{orig}}, and it gains where the original criteria demand an unstated protocol, as in press_by_number, swap_blocks and make_kong. The exposed library loses where it had learned that protocol, and on tasks whose criteria changes mostly fix defects or relax thresholds the two criteria give nearly the same scores.

4.2.2 Swapping the Criteria that Are Read

Setup.

We then let the learner read CfaithC^{\text{faith}} instead (ten tasks, five rounds) and compare the resulting library ℒCEfaith\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} with ℒCEorig\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{orig}} on the same ten tasks, each judged by the criteria its learner read and by the other.

Results.

Figure 5 shows that each exposed library does well only under the criteria it read: ℒCEorig\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{orig}} falls from 57.0% to 45.0% under CfaithC^{\text{faith}}, and ℒCEfaith\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} from 65.0% to 13.5% under CorigC^{\text{orig}}. The fall is steeper for ℒCEfaith\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} because the two directions differ: CfaithC^{\text{faith}} mostly removes or relaxes the hidden rules and thresholds of CorigC^{\text{orig}}, so moving ℒCEorig\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{orig}} to CfaithC^{\text{faith}} loosens the verification, whereas moving ℒCEfaith\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} to CorigC^{\text{orig}} adds back every rule the library never saw. The score follows the criteria that were read even where they are looser: having read CfaithC^{\text{faith}}, the library no longer sets the bottle upright in pour_by_language, which CorigC^{\text{orig}} requires, and solves 19 of its 20 test layouts under CfaithC^{\text{faith}} but none under CorigC^{\text{orig}}. This does not tell which criteria are right, which section 4.2.1 addresses, but it shows that the score of exposure does not carry between two criteria that score the same instruction.

4.2.3 Synthesis and Implications

  • •

    Exposure makes self-improvement fit the criteria rather than learn the instructed task. A higher score from reading the criteria is commonly taken as faster learning of the task. A learner that reads the criteria, however, revises the library until it passes the verifier it reads, so the library learns the task only as far as the criteria agree with the instruction. Under instruction-faithful criteria the exposed library loses successes that the success-only library gains, and each exposed library scores best only under the criteria it read: on press_by_number it solves all 20 layouts under CorigC^{\text{orig}} and none under CfaithC^{\text{faith}}, and the library that read CfaithC^{\text{faith}} solves 65.0% of its test episodes under CfaithC^{\text{faith}} but 13.5% under CorigC^{\text{orig}}. Self-improvement should therefore be measured without exposure by default, with the success rate under instruction-faithful criteria reported alongside: a robot in the real world has no criteria code, so the part of a gain that survives a change of criteria is the part to expect there.

  • •

    Exposure changes what the learner writes down. A learner that reads the criteria can explain a failure by the condition it violated, so its experience is phrased in the terms of one verifier; a learner that sees only success has to find a physical cause, and its rules are closer to regularities of the robot. About a third of the exposed memory entries cite the criteria code, and none of the success-only ones do.

4.3 Reusing the Library: What Carries Over

Finally, we carry the libraries to new tasks in RoboDojo and to two further benchmarks.

4.3.1 Across Tasks within RoboDojo

Setup.

We distill the libraries of ten learned tasks into one library per setting and apply it to ten target tasks that none of the source tasks covers, paired with the empty library on the same layouts.

Results.

Both settings help on the target tasks (first row of table 2): the empty library solves 65 of 200 episodes, the success-only library 80 and the exposed one 71. The 14.2-point lead of exposure on its own tasks does not reappear.

4.3.2 Across Benchmarks

Setup.

We apply the same libraries, translated to each target’s prompt and primitives, on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365, whose primitives we aligned with RoboDojo’s. On LIBERO-PRO the empty library already solves 34 of the 40 tasks on all five seeds, so we use the 6 others, with ten seeds each. On RoboCasa365 we also distill one library per setting from other RoboCasa365 tasks, as an in-benchmark reference.

Results.

The libraries from RoboDojo add little on either benchmark (table 2): 48 and 46 of 60 episodes against 45 on LIBERO-PRO, and 24 and 24 of 100 against 22 on RoboCasa365. The libraries distilled within RoboCasa365 do better, 33 (w/o CE) and 29 (w/ CE) of 100.

4.3.3 Synthesis and Implications

  • •

    What exposure adds is specific to the task it was learned on. One might expect the setting that scores higher on its own tasks to transfer better. It does not: the lead of exposure disappears on target tasks. Exposed experience carries the conditions and precision needed to pass one task’s criteria, which become noise or overhead elsewhere, whereas rules about the gripper hold across tasks.

  • •

    Experience transfers where the bottleneck is shared. Within a benchmark the robot, the scenes and perception stay the same, and learned rules carry over. Across benchmarks the general part of the experience is already covered by the target’s prompt, while what the target lacks has no counterpart in the source, so the transferred skills go unused; experience gathered on the target benchmark, even on other tasks, addresses its own bottleneck and helps.

5 Limitations and Future Work

The instruction-faithful criteria are ours, and the feedback is simulated.  CfaithC^{\text{faith}} serves as our proxy for the success the instruction asks for, SτS_{\tau}. Neither setting’s libraries saw the rewritten criteria when they were written; rules and types were fixed in advance; a second seed was judged independently and every flipped episode checked. Still, only RoboDojo’s criteria were rewritten, and success-only feedback in simulation is cleaner than the success a human or a VLM reports for a robot in the real world, which has no criteria code. Next steps are an independent review, released criteria code, rewritten criteria for a second benchmark, and VLM success detection in place of the simulator’s success [11].

Exposure is studied at two levels, as current systems implement it.  Most existing systems sit at intermediate levels (rule descriptions, published scoring tables, partial thresholds), which we did not study separately. A next step is to expose these levels one at a time and measure how the gain under CorigC^{\text{orig}}, and its loss under CfaithC^{\text{faith}}, grow with what the learner reads.

Samples are small and the mechanisms are inferred.  Each task has 20 test layouts, so quantitative claims use pooled results and single tasks are described only qualitatively; and distillation variance was not estimated. The accounts of what exposure writes into the library, of what carries over and of how the actor uses transferred libraries rest on entry text, skill calls and action statistics, not on ablations. Next steps are repeated distillations and ablations that remove or swap individual entries, such as the re-measuring entries of the distilled w/ CE library or the memory entries of a translated library.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we studied what a self-improving embodied agent learns when it reads the success criteria, by comparing one self-improvement loop with and without Criteria Exposure, under the benchmark’s own and instruction-faithful criteria, and on new tasks and benchmarks. Our results show that self-improvement from success alone is real and survives a change of criteria, whereas the score that Criteria Exposure adds comes mainly from satisfying the criteria that were read: it appears only where the criteria and the instruction disagree, disappears under instruction-faithful criteria, and across benchmarks neither the exposed nor the success-only library gives a clear gain, while only in-benchmark experience helps. These findings provide a more careful reading of reported self-improvement gains on embodied benchmarks and practical guidance for measuring them: use the feedback a robot receives in the real world, and judge by criteria that verify what the instruction says. A robot in the real world never sees its verifier; the agent we measure should not either.

Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier?
Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

Appendix

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Experimental protocol

Benchmark.  RoboDojo’s simulation track uses a dual-arm ARX-X5 with RGB observations only; its 42 tasks span five capability dimensions. The 20 tasks on which the zero-shot actor solves fewer than half of the episodes of the official evaluation seed, with five stronger ones, make the 25 compared tasks (table 4). Every run uses one version of RoboDojo (Table 3); task source, criteria, leaderboard script and evaluation layouts are identical file by file across the checkouts we compare.

Conditions.  The actor’s model, primitives and prompt are the same in every condition. The learner with Criteria Exposure reads the criteria code, each episode’s score and its passed stages; the one without sees full trajectories and success only. All conditions are compared over five rounds of improvement (rounds 0–5). The groups (Appendix B) rest on reading the code, the learners’ diagnoses and the failed rollouts.

Layouts.  Development reruns layouts 0–4 of official evaluation seed 1 every round; the test layouts are layouts 0–19 of seed 0 (500 episodes per condition), which no learner sees.

Statistics.  Development batches are noisy: rerunning one library on one layout changes the verdict in 4% of cases, and the two round-0 batches of the same empty library differ in at least 13% of episodes. We therefore draw conclusions from the test layouts and pooled curves, and read single-task development curves only qualitatively.

A.2 Implementation and settings

Actor. GPT-6 Astra writes one code cell per MLLM call against PyRUA-Lean’s frozen robo API [29]: RGB perception (SAM 3 [7] and multi-view measurement) and motion primitives, with no VLA policy, depth or simulator state. The library is installed as a package library/: cells import its skills, and its live memory entries are appended to the prompt.

Library. A skill is a function of robo that imports only standard modules, numpy and other library modules, does no I/O and returns {"ok": …, "why": …, …}. A memory entry is ## {task}-<stage>-<nnn> followed by stage, symptom, applies, do, status and evidence. A task’s library holds at most 40,000 characters, all of which the actor reads.

Learner. Claude Code reads the session, the task’s dev runs, the API source and, with Criteria Exposure, the task’s criteria; it writes only the candidate library, its verification rollouts and its notes. Without Criteria Exposure, criteria, scores and stages are removed from the evidence.

Acceptance and rollback. A candidate may change only the task’s own directory, must keep every memory entry identifier, must cite a judged rollout or dev batch for each entry newly marked dev_verified, and must pass the static skill rules and the size limit; none of this looks at success, and no candidate was refused. The active revision rolls back to the best earlier complete batch when a complete batch has two or more fewer successes; ties go to the batch that passed more stages, and a batch with an episode lost to infrastructure neither triggers a rollback nor becomes the best.

A.3 Evaluation details

The 25 learned tasks are grouped by whether their criteria were rewritten. Layouts that the benchmark marks unstable are replaced by the next layout in the official order. Under dual judging an episode ends early only when both criteria have reached a verdict, so neither verdict is truncated.

A.4 Tasks

Appendix B Comparing Criteria with Instructions in RoboDojo

Criteria mechanism.

RoboDojo criteria are sequences of stages: check stages in order, final_check at termination, and trigger_check, evaluated only at the step its condition becomes true; query requires exact counts and fails the episode for good once a count is exceeded; conditions nest with alternating AND and OR. Of the 42 tasks, 33 require both arms to return within 15 cm and 20° of home, while only 5 instructions ask for a reset.

Method.

For each task we compare gen_instruction, run_reward, get_score and the configuration, grade the severity as high, medium or low, and confirm by hand; the review is mainly a static reading of the code.

Types.

The type names are ours.

  • •

    Hidden rule: the criteria verify conditions the instruction does not state (order, counts, relative position), e.g. the button protocol of press_by_number or the tile to draw in make_kong.

  • •

    Hard threshold: the tolerance is stricter than clearly satisfying the instruction requires, e.g. 97% of the liquid in pour_liquid_into_cup.

  • •

    Timing, event triggers and irreversibility: verification at one step only, or permanent failure once an event happens, e.g. pouring judged only when the bottle returns upright; a third press in press_by_number.

  • •

    Criteria defect: the criteria code or an asset annotation is wrong, e.g. mug 14 in hang_mugs_random, the bug in solve_equation.

  • •

    Extra end state: an end state the instruction does not mention, e.g. in make_toast the two remaining slices must stay on the bread shelf.

  • •

    Loose criteria: trajectories that skip the action the instruction asks for are accepted, e.g. sweep_blocks accepts blocks picked up without the broom.

  • •

    Contradiction: the criteria require the opposite of the instruction, e.g. in classify_objects_by_language the categories are named after asset folders, so a chocolate bunny counts as a wooden toy.

Counts.

23 tasks are consistent and 19 inconsistent (hidden rule 9, hidden rule and hard threshold 5, hard threshold 3, contradiction 1, defect 1); with solve_equation, whose criteria have a bug, 20 tasks and 26 variants are criteria-limited. By type, at medium or high severity: hidden rule 13, hard threshold 13, timing and events 10, defect 9, extra end state 5, loose criteria 4, contradiction 3. Other typical cases are make_kong (a tile must be drawn) and build_tower (only one configuration is accepted).

Published rules.

The task descriptions and scoring tables on the RoboDojo website publish part of these rules, for example the button order of press_by_number; the recipes of EmbodiedEvo and HexaShell come from there [18, 13]. Table 5 gives the tasks by type. A task is criteria-limited only if the manual review confirms that its criteria and its instruction disagree; the table also lists the findings for tasks that the review kept as faithful.

Appendix C Instruction-faithful Criteria

Rules.

(1) Change only run_reward and get_score, never the instruction. (2) Keep the return of both arms. (3) Remove or relax hidden rules. (4) Fix defects. (5) Tighten loose criteria where the simulator state detects the difference reliably. (6) Relax hard thresholds to what still clearly satisfies the instruction, listing old and new values. (7) Correct asset annotations in memory only. (8) Leave the original repository untouched. New criteria primitives check distance and orientation on the same feature, containment in an elliptic cylinder, and connected towers.

Validation.

Offline unit tests; shadow judging and reruns on seed 0; on seed 2 both criteria judge the same episodes independently (an episode ends only when both have a verdict), and every flipped episode was checked by hand.

Decisions of our own.

“Tighten” in fasten_screws means a nut sinking at least 35 mm. We also decided what counts as a tower in build_tower and which edges of the laptop may face down in store_laptop_and_headphones. Appendix C lists every change.

Changes from CorigC^{\text{orig}} to CfaithC^{\text{faith}}. Type: D, defect fixed; H, hidden rule removed; R, hard threshold relaxed; T, loose criterion tightened. A _random variant receives the same change unless marked. Conditions not listed, including the return of both arms, are unchanged. Asset annotations are corrected in memory only. Liquid thresholds are shares of the poured liquid in the target and left in the bottle.
